source.title: Learning from Negative Examples: Why Warning-Framed Training Data Teaches What It Warns Against

record.tranche_reason: Uses SAE feature measurements and a probe to examine whether an LLM has identifiable features, a different method from the toy-model superposition experiments. It does not test feature-over-capacity storage or superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper reports warning-training behavior and interventions, but those test learning from warning-framed data, not the claim versions about superposition or polysemanticity. The SAE findings bear narrowly on V4: the paper identifies a feature in Gemma-2-2B and tests its activation across contexts. It does not measure sparse-feature recovery quality or feature spread across neurons.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained Gemma Scope SAEs as a tool to compare feature activations between warning-framed, direct and safe code generation in Gemma-2-2B. It assumes SAE features are meaningful units and never asks whether features are superposed, how many neurons they spread across, or how well the SAE recovers them. Its results bear on why warning-framed data teaches its content, not on any superposition version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is largely right. The authors also conclude three further things. First, warning-framed (L1) training yields 76.7% target content vs 83.3% for direct training, which is not significantly different. Second, prompting and inference-time feature ablation fail to correct the behavior, while training-time ablation (CAFT) brings it to 0%. Third, conversational preambles can evade linear-probe detection ('stealth slip').
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes SAE activations and probe generalization in Gemma-2-2B; it does not use the original toy-network setup or measure superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different feature activation for safe contexts than for direct and warning-framed target-content contexts.

fits_no_version.finding: Of 47 high-activation SAE candidate features, only 11 pass Model-X knockoff FDR control at q=0.1. The paper calls this consistent with roughly 25% of high-activity latents being genuine.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Only a minority of high-activation SAE latents carry task-relevant signal after false-discovery control (bears loosely on SAE feature reliability).

fits_no_version.finding: Inference-time clamping of four SAE features (or of Feature #8684, per Figure 5) leaves the target rate at 88%. The authors read this as the behavior being distributed across redundant pathways.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Behavior-relevant computation is distributed across many SAE features, so single-feature ablation does not remove it.

record.problems: The mechanistic analysis uses one model at 2B parameters and one SAE setup. The paper does not report uncertainty for the feature magnitudes or probe result, and it does not quantify feature overlap geometry or establish that the SAE features are complete or canonical.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were extracted for warning-training rates, prompting, or ablation outcomes because those results concern learning and suppressing vulnerable-code behavior, not the claim versions about superposition or feature units.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, no capacity, sparsity or geometry measurements.
All: no analysis of capacity competition or polysemanticity.
All: no analysis of how polysemantic neurons arise.
All: SAEs are used as a pretrained tool. No measurement of feature spread across neurons, sparsity, or reconstruction fidelity.
All: completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not examined. The authors themselves caveat that 'identified features may be proxies'.
All: feature dimensionality is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4 link and 'supports' label are not justified: the SAE analysis presupposes SAE features rather than testing their existence or recovery. There are internal inconsistencies worth flagging. §7.2 names features #4817, #13950, #1692 and #2527 as the ablated features, but the Figure 5 caption says Feature #8684 was ablated. Llama-3.2-3B is cited to the Llama 2 paper. No uncertainty is given for the SAE magnitudes or the probe result. The study is a single-author preprint.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, more features than dimensions, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether limited capacity causes polysemanticity or allocates dedicated dimensions to important features.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Feature spread across neurons, feature sparsity or recovery fidelity, and generalization beyond the tested SAE and model.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of the model's representation.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions or multi-dimensional.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured Layer 20, width 16k SAE Feature #8684 activation during direct target-content generation.
rows.note: The paper associates this feature with code execution patterns and reports high activation in direct generations.
rows.check: Activation of one SAE feature in direct-generation context (150–180 vs <20 safe). This compares contexts for a feature assumed to be real. It does not measure feature spread, sparsity or SAE recovery, so it has no bearing on V4.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured Layer 20, width 16k SAE Feature #8684 activation during warning-framed target-content generation.
rows.note: The paper reports comparable activation in warning-framed and direct generations.
rows.check: Same feature in the warning-framed context. This bears on the paper's 'shared representation' claim, not on superposition or on SAE recoverability.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured Layer 20, width 16k SAE Feature #8684 activation during safe-content generation.
rows.note: This is the safe-context comparison for the reported direct and warning-framed activations.
rows.check: Safe-context control value (<20) for the same comparison. It is not a measure of any superposition version.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Trained a linear probe on direct generations and evaluated it on warning-framed outputs.
rows.note: The paper says this generalization confirms that the activation patterns are indistinguishable.
rows.check: Linear probe trained on direct outputs and tested on warning outputs (100% confidence). This is about the two contexts being representationally alike, not about superposition or dictionary features.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Applied Model-X knockoff false-discovery-rate control to high-activation candidate SAE features.
rows.measure: Candidate features passing the knockoff filter
rows.note: The four features used in ablation experiments are also listed among those passing the filter.
rows.check: This is a selection/validation step: 11 of 47 candidate features pass a knockoff FDR filter. It is the study's own feature-screening method, not a test of whether LLMs contain SAE-recoverable sparse features. Also, the 'observed' state has no defined effect to observe.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Gemma-2-2B, tested direct and warning-framed contexts
reader_labels.reason: SAE Feature #8684 shows high activation in both target-content contexts and low activation in the safe context; the probe generalizes to warning outputs (r1, r2, r3, r4, r5). This is narrow evidence for SAE-identifiable features, not for feature sparsity or spread across neurons.
